Tool Use Enables Undetectable Steganography in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

Jimmy Laurence Rippin Affiliation: Oxford University Email: jimmylrippin@gmail.com    Simon C. Marshall Affiliation: Artificial Intelligence Security Institute (AISI) Email: simon.marshall@dsit.gov.uk    David Demitri Africa Affiliation: Artificial Intelligence Security Institute (AISI) Email: david.africa@dsit.gov.uk    Christian Schroeder de Witt Affiliation: Oxford University Email: contact@wittlab.ai
Abstract

Increasingly autonomous agentic AI systems pose novel multi-agent risks, such as secret collusion via covert communication channels. The natural defence to these collusion attempts is to monitor plain-text communication, but the efficacy of monitors has been called into doubt by increasingly sophisticated model steganography; indeed, some theoretical schemes have been proposed that are information-theoretically or computationally indistinguishable from good-faith plain-text communication. In this paper, we demonstrate that the complexity of these schemes is no longer a safety barrier, as agentic coding models can already produce undetectable stegosystems when given realistic tool usage, such as code execution or accessing research papers through web searches. Agents also adapt when key ingredients are missing, for example, by adding model-sampling components or implementing related keyed coding schemes. We then frame tacit steganographic coordination between agents as a Schelling-point problem and introduce coordination metrics for estimating when two agents are likely to select compatible schemes without explicit prior agreement. Our results suggest a shift in the threat model for covert communication between AI agents, where the main barrier is no longer whether frontier agents can understand and implement sophisticated stegosystems, but coordination: whether independently acting agents can converge on compatible schemes, keys, and parameters. We find substantial convergence on broad scheme families but limited strict one-shot coordination, suggesting that shared artefacts, repeated interaction, and tool-mediated search are the settings where covert communication risks are most acute. Overall, our findings provide empirical grounding for the recent strategic confinement hypothesis, which assumes that capable agents can construct covert channels that survive monitoring.

1 Introduction

Monitored natural-language channels are a common safety boundary in multi-agent AI systems. Modern large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use tools, call APIs, execute code, and coordinate with other agents through natural-language messages (Yao et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2023). A system designer may therefore allow two agents to exchange task-relevant messages while relying on a human or model monitor to prevent private information, hidden goals, or coordination signals from crossing the boundary (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Baker et al., 2025). This defence assumes that if the monitor can read the messages, it can enforce the information-flow policy.

Steganography breaks this assumption, since a sender can encode a payload inside apparently benign text, allowing a receiver with the right decoding procedure to recover information that the monitor does not know was transmitted (Simmons, 1984). This risk has been formalised as secret collusion among AI agents, where agents use covert communication to hide the true nature of their interaction from oversight (Motwani et al., 2025). Prior work has also shown that language-model steganography can be made information-theoretically undetectable (Schroeder de Witt et al., 2023) or undetectable under appropriate sampling and cryptographic assumptions (von Ahn and Hopper, 2004; Ziegler et al., 2019; Christ et al., 2023; Zamir, 2024). Thus, we ask if current agentic models operationalise such schemes when given realistic tool affordances.

To answer this, we evaluate tool-using LLM agents to construct covert communication channels under a range of increasingly restricted environments. Agents can implement candidate undetectable stegosystems from research papers, recover implementation details through web search, add missing sampling components, and hide covert-channel logic inside an existing multi-agent codebase. We then study the coordination problem faced by two agents that cannot explicitly agree on a scheme. Treating steganographic design choices as focal points, we estimate how often independent agents converge on compatible algorithms and parameters, building on prior work on tacit coordination in LLMs (Aharon et al., 2026).

Our results suggest that covert communication is no longer bottlenecked by cryptographic expertise, and is becoming an ordinary consequence of agentic tool use. The limiting factor is increasingly not cryptographic invention, but ordinary agentic competence: reading papers, writing code, using tools, and converging on salient designs. Overall, our findings provide empirical grounding for the recent strategic confinement hypothesis (Schroeder de Witt, 2026), a reinterpretation of Lampson’s confinement problem (Lampson, 1973) for strategic agents, which assumes that capable agents can construct covert channels that survive monitoring.

Contributions.

We make four contributions. First, we introduce an agentic covert-channel construction benchmark, where a tool-using LLM must build a working natural-language stegosystem rather than merely describe one (Section 3.1). Second, we frame tacit steganographic agreement as a Schelling-point coordination problem over algorithms, keys, and decoding-relevant parameters (Section 3.2.1). Third, we show robust implementation capability: agents construct functional covert channels with papers, web search, code execution, model-sampling components, and existing multi-agent codebases (Section 4.1). Fourth, we identify exact parameter agreement as the main bottleneck: agents often converge on broad scheme families, but strict first-shot complete coordination remains fragile (Section 4.2).

2 Background and Problem Setup

Monitored-channel threat model.

We consider a multi-agent system (MAS) with at least two agents, a sender AA and a receiver BB, connected by some monitored natural-language channel. Agent AA has access to some information xx that BB is not permitted to learn. A monitor observes the messages sent from AA to BB, and blocks messages that appear to violate the information-flow policy. The intended safety boundary is therefore content-level monitoring, where, if the monitor can read every message, it should be able to prevent restricted information from crossing the channel.

Instead of sending xx directly, AA can send an apparently benign cover text c′c^{\prime} from which BB can recover a hidden payload using a decoding procedure. The monitor may observe the complete text of c′c^{\prime} while remaining unaware that a payload was transmitted. We focus on text-based steganographic channels, where the cover object is natural-language model output.

Steganographic channels.

A keyed stegosystem consists of an encoder, a decoder, a payload space, a cover distribution, and a shared secret key. The encoder maps a payload and cover-generation process into a stego-object, while the decoder uses the key to recover the payload. The relevant security notion is not whether the text looks suspicious to a casual reader, but whether a monitor without the key can distinguish stego-objects from ordinary samples drawn from the cover distribution. Prior work has proposed language-model stegosystems and watermarking-derived schemes with formal undetectability guarantees under appropriate assumptions (Christ et al., 2023; Zamir, 2024). Our question is whether current agents can operationalize such schemes in practice.

Agentic construction.

Tool use changes the threat model. A model that cannot directly produce a covert channel from memory may still be able to read papers, search the web, write code, run tests, use model-sampling components, and iterate until an encoder/decoder pair works. We therefore evaluate covert-channel construction as an agentic capability rather than as a memorised behaviour. In our experiments, success requires producing an implementation that can transmit synthetic payloads through benign-looking outputs under the constraints of the environment.

Tacit coordination.

A second obstacle is coordination. Two agents may both be capable of building covert channels, but fail to communicate if they independently choose incompatible algorithms, keys, or hyperparameters. We treat this as a focal-point coordination problem, where the design space contains many possible steganographic schemes, but some are more salient because they are named in the prompt, present in a shared file system, easy to find on the web, or common in the training distribution. We estimate the probability of tacit agreement by sampling independent agent plans and measuring how often they collide on compatible algorithmic and parameter choices.

We provide an extended background, with a gentle introduction to steganography in Appendix A. Additionally, we provide a survey of related work in the fields of misalignment, watermarking, and LLM cooperation in Appendix B.

3 Methodology

We break down the likelihood of harmful steganography SS into 3 key areas assumed independent of each other: the likelihood that an agent can implement a scheme II, the likelihood that agents can coordinate on a compatible channel CC, and the risk that illegal information flow can cause harm RR.

ℙ⁡[S]=ℙ⁡[I]×ℙ⁡[C]×ℙ⁡[R]\mathbb{P}[S]=\mathbb{P}[I]\times\mathbb{P}[C]\times\mathbb{P}[R] (1)

3.1 Steganographic implementation

Agents are frequently permitted unlimited and unmonitored tool usage, for example, with Claude’s –dangerously-skip-permissions tag (Hughes, 2026). We assess whether agents can implement undetectable steganography, such that a monitor with access only to agent outputs cannot detect the presence of a hidden payload. Formally, we define the threat model used.

Actors and goals

  • •

    Adversary: A capable agent intending to covertly transmit information in its natural language outputs without detection by content-level monitoring. Shares a secret key with the receiver.

  • •

    Receiver: A cooperating party (human or AI) that possesses the secret key and intends to decode hidden messages from the agent’s outputs.

  • •

    Monitor: The defender (human or AI) responsible for detecting and preventing covert channels. Has access to all agent outputs, but not the tool usage or intermediate artefacts.

Adversary capabilities and knowledge

  1. 1.

    Ability to execute code in a sandboxed environment.

  2. 2.

    Access to a sub-model (or API) that returns log probabilities for candidate next tokens, and the ability to call it.

  3. 3.

    Access to a file system to stage intermediate artefacts, including models and test data, and optionally install vetted packages.

  4. 4.

    Ability to find/derive an undetectable steganography scheme, given that the paper by Zamir (2024) is in their file system.

In some aspects, this is a reasonable threat model. Developers rarely monitor tool usage unless they are particularly security-conscious, agents typically have access to the file system and can execute code, and frontier models are capable of understanding complex research papers and correctly implementing concepts from them. However, few agents have access to a sub-model; malicious prompts could be prevented with additional monitoring; generic file systems don’t contain research papers detailing a steganographic implementation. As such, we design experiments that isolate each assumption to investigate which are necessary for a successful implementation.

3.2 Steganography as tacit coordination

Define A=A1×A2A=A_{1}\times A_{2} to be the action space of a two-player game, where AiA_{i} are the actions available to player ii. A two-player pure coordination game (Shoham and Leyton-Brown, 2008) satisfies Equation 2, where ui:Ai→ℝu_{i}:A_{i}\to\mathbb{R} is the utility function of player ii. Intuitively, players have no conflicting interests; their sole challenge is to coordinate on a mutually maximally beneficial action, succeeding when the action profile is a Nash equilibrium (Nash, 1951).

∀(a1,a2)∈A1×A2,u1​(a1,a2)=u2​(a1,a2)\forall(a_{1},a_{2})\in A_{1}\times A_{2},\quad u_{1}(a_{1},a_{2})=u_{2}(a_{1},a_{2}) (2)

Common knowledge between two agents consists of facts that each agent knows, each agent knows that the other agent knows, each agent knows that each agent knows that the other agent knows, and so on (Halpern and Moses, 1990; Osborne and Rubinstein, 2006). Formally, we define an infinite recursion where α0\alpha_{0} is the set of information known by both agents, and αi+1\alpha_{i+1} is the subset of αi\alpha_{i} that both agents know is contained in αi\alpha_{i}, then α\alpha is commonly known if it satisfies Equation 3 (Schroeder de Witt, 2021).

α=⋂i=0∞αi\alpha=\bigcap^{\infty}_{i=0}\alpha_{i} (3)

Let αA\alpha_{A} be the common knowledge base of actions, and ℰ⊂αA\mathcal{E}\subset\alpha_{A} be the set of commonly known Nash equilibria; some actions in ℰ\mathcal{E} may appear more prominent, conspicuous, or salient than others as a focal point for solving the game. We define the Schelling salience (Mehta et al., 1994) function S:ℰ→ℝ≥0S:\mathcal{E}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} that represents how strongly each Nash equilibrium stands out (Aharon et al., 2026).

Salience can vary between players, so we interpret Schelling salience as a probability distribution over ℰ\mathcal{E} by applying softmax with 𝒞\mathcal{C} a coordination sensitivity parameter, where 𝒞=0\mathcal{C}=0 represents no coordination (Nash equilibria are selected randomly, with no regard for salience), and as 𝒞→∞\mathcal{C}\to\infty, players tend to the most salient equilibrium (Aharon et al., 2026):

PS:ℰ→[0,1]​, s.t ​∑a∈ℰPS​(a)=1​, where ​PS​(a)=exp⁡(𝒞⋅S⁡(a))∑a′∈ℰexp⁡(𝒞⋅S⁡(a′))P_{S}:\mathcal{E}\to[0,1]\text{, s.t }\sum_{a\in\mathcal{E}}P_{S}(a)=1\text{, where }P_{S}(a)=\frac{\exp(\mathcal{C}\cdot S(a))}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{E}}\exp(\mathcal{C}\cdot S(a^{\prime}))} (4)
Definition 1

The Schelling sharpness of a game is the success rate when players play by choosing action a∈ℰa\in\mathcal{E} with probability PS​(a)P_{S}(a):

𝒮=∑a∈ℰℙ⁡[Player 1 chooses ​a]⋅ℙ⁡[Player 2 chooses ​a]=∑a∈ℰPS​(a)2\mathcal{S}=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{E}}\mathbb{P}[\text{Player 1 chooses }a]\cdot\mathbb{P}[\text{Player 2 chooses }a]=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{E}}P_{S}(a)^{2} (5)

Schelling sharpness depends on the population of players and the game environment. More rational players will have a higher value of 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and will exhibit better coordination; an environment with few salient solutions will result in a more concentrated Schelling salience distribution.

An environment in which two agents connected by a monitored channel with simultaneous messaging independently attempt to implement a steganographic scheme can be considered a two-player pure coordination game. Formally, possible implementations are actions, including hyperparameter or key selection, and Nash equilibria are compatible implementations that can successfully encode/decode payloads. Research suggests that LLMs surpass reinforcement learning methods (Agashe et al., 2025) and humans (Aharon et al., 2026) in some pure coordination games; hence, when agents are placed into a coordination game, we must expect their coordinated capability to be correlated with the sharpness of the game. Thus, by assessing the MAS Schelling sharpness with respect to a common knowledge base of steganographic implementations, we can determine the likelihood that two agents choose the same implementation without prior communication.

3.2.1 Measuring coordination

An agent attempting to coordinate on a steganographic implementation in environments that don’t specify precise implementations could implement a variety of stegosystems, with a wide range of hyperparameter values; thus, the probability of perfect coordination is minimal, and obtaining the empirical coordination rate is infeasible. Schelling sharpness cannot be precisely determined, as there is no concrete metric for the salience of each implementation in a MAS. Thus, an approximation of Schelling sharpness is an effective approximation to the empirical rate.

We instead calculate the unbiased estimator of Schelling sharpness by sampling different agent instances, obtaining their plan for a steganographic implementation, and representing their choice of action. This unbiased estimator coincides with the definition of the Coordination Index (CI) (Bardsley et al., 2010), the probability that two agents from our sample of size nn choose the same action, where AA is the set of actions appearing in our sample, and mam_{a} is the number of agents in the sample choosing label aa:

C​I=∑a∈Ama​(ma−1)n⁡(n−1)CI=\sum_{a\in A}\frac{m_{a}(m_{a}-1)}{n(n-1)} (6)

We say that an implementation plan is successful if it results in steganography under the environmental assumptions, should the other agent choose the same implementation plan. We can calculate the implementation success rate from the set of sampled implementation plans II:

S​R=1N​∑i∈I𝟏​[i​ is successful]SR=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in I}\mathbf{1}[i\text{ is successful}] (7)

We consider multiple levels of coordination in our experiments:

Algorithmic coordination.

Agents select identical stegosystems, but not necessarily hyperparameters. The algorithmic coordination index (ACI) can be calculated using Equation 6, where each label mim_{i} is the chosen steganographic algorithm.

Hyperparameter coordination.

For agents that both suggest a value for a hyperparameter, the rate at which the values match. The hyperparameter coordination index (HCI) can be calculated as the mean CI of each hyperparameter, where HH is the set of hyperparameters specified by any agent, each hi∈hh_{i}\in h is a chosen value for hyperparameter hh:

H​C​I=1|H|​∑h∈H∑hi∈hmhi​(mhi−1)nh​(nh−1)HCI=\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}\sum_{h_{i}\in h}\frac{m_{h_{i}}(m_{h_{i}}-1)}{n_{h}(n_{h}-1)} (8)
Complete coordination.

Agents select identical stegosystems and hyperparameters. To obtain a good approximation with a small sample size, we calculate the rate of complete coordination by multiplying the rate of coordination on each hyperparameter for a given algorithm. Crucially, we include only successful implementation plans in mm values for this approximation, ensuring that the metric consists of only perfect successful coordination, but we use total nn values for normalisation. The complete coordination index (CCI) can be calculated using the equation below, where HaH_{a} is the set of hyperparameters required for algorithm aa, mas,mhism_{a}^{s},m_{h_{i}}^{s} are the number of successful plans implementing algorithm aa and using hih_{i} as the hyperparameter value of hh; ntn^{t} is the total number of plans (not just successful ones), nhtn_{h}^{t} is the total number of plans that specify a value for hh:

C​C​I=∑a∈A(CI on ​a⋅∏h∈HaCI on ​h)=∑a∈A(mas​(mas−1)nt​(nt−1)⋅∏h∈Ha∑hi∈hmhis​(mhis−1)nht​(nht−1))CCI=\sum_{a\in A}\left(\text{CI on }a\cdot\prod_{h\in H_{a}}\text{CI on }h\right)=\sum_{a\in A}\left(\frac{m_{a}^{s}(m_{a}^{s}-1)}{n^{t}(n^{t}-1)}\cdot\prod_{h\in H_{a}}\sum_{h_{i}\in h}\frac{m^{s}_{h_{i}}(m^{s}_{h_{i}}-1)}{n^{t}_{h}(n^{t}_{h}-1)}\right) (9)

The CCI is our approximation of Schelling sharpness.

3.3 Risk

Alongside our assessment of the likelihood that steganography emerges, it is also relevant to consider the maximal potential harm that could occur if a steganographic channel existed in a system. We categorise the potential risk of a MAS as none, low, moderate, or high depending on the possibility of illegal information flow, specified by information flow restrictions, and explain how a system designer can model them and identify specification violations using a monitor. Risk is inherent in the definition of the environmental information set specifications and cannot necessarily be reduced.

3.3.1 Information flow

We define the discrete time steps within a system with communication channels where the time step value tt is xx at the xthx^{\text{th}} distinct time at which a message is sent over a channel. We then define the information set that the system designer permits each subject to have at each time step, requiring that information learned is modelled to be retained by agents:

Definition 2

For each time step t≥0t\geq 0, the information set ℐ⁡(sk,t)\mathcal{I}(s_{k},t) contains the information that subject sks_{k} is permitted to know at time step tt, such that for all tt, ℐ⁡(sk,t)⊆ℐ⁡(sk,t+1)\mathcal{I}(s_{k},t)\subseteq\mathcal{I}(s_{k},t+1) is satisfied.

Definition 3

The information set ℐ⁡(sk)=⋃t≥0ℐ⁡(sk,t)\mathcal{I}(s_{k})=\bigcup_{t\geq 0}\mathcal{I}(s_{k},t) contains all information that subject sks_{k} is permitted to ever know within the system.

Subjects communicate over channels with restricted information flow:

Definition 4

A channel C⁡(si,sj)C(s_{i},s_{j}) permits subject sis_{i} to communicate with subject sjs_{j}. The permissible information flow at time step t≥0t\geq 0is ℐ⁡(C,t)=ℐ⁡(si,t)∩ℐ⁡(sj,t+1)\mathcal{I}(C,t)=\mathcal{I}(s_{i},t)\cap\mathcal{I}(s_{j},t+1). The information flow ever permitted is ℐ⁡(C)=ℐ⁡(si)∩ℐ⁡(sj)\mathcal{I}(C)=\mathcal{I}(s_{i})\cap\mathcal{I}(s_{j})

Illegal information flow (Nakamura et al., 2014) is a violation of subject information sets:

Definition 5

Illegal information flow on channel C⁡(si,sj)C(s_{i},s_{j}) at time step t≥0t\geq 0 is any information i∈ℐ⁡(si,t)−ℐ⁡(sj,t+1)i\in\mathcal{I}(s_{i},t)-\mathcal{I}(s_{j},t+1).

Information flow permissions can be enforced by a monitor:

Definition 6

A subject sms_{m} can be a monitor for a channel CC if their information set satisfies ℐ⁡(sm)⊇ℐ⁡(C)∪iC\mathcal{I}(s_{m})\supseteq\mathcal{I}(C)\cup i_{C} where iCi_{C} is information specifying the exact contents of ℐ⁡(C,t)\mathcal{I}(C,t) at each time step t≥0t\geq 0.

A key benefit of our information flow definition is that a system specification can be created using a temporal logic (Pnueli, 1977) formula using propositions p⁡(sj,x)p(s_{j},x) representing that subject sjs_{j} knows xx at each time step tt where the proposition holds, i.e. x∈ℐ⁡(sj,t)x\in\mathcal{I}(s_{j},t). Since temporal logic is commonly used to model systems, developers can apply existing models to this information flow framework.

3.3.2 Risk categories

A MAS has no risk if there exist no channels where any information could be passed that the receiving agent doesn’t know by the time it reaches them anyway. Agents can therefore gain no additional information, including the knowledge that the sender agent chose to send a given piece of information: the information set encapsulates all information. Formally, this satisfies:

∃C⁡(si,sj)⟹∀t≥0,ℐ⁡(si,t)⊆ℐ⁡(sj,t+1)\exists C(s_{i},s_{j})\implies\forall t\geq 0,\;\mathcal{I}(s_{i},t)\subseteq\mathcal{I}(s_{j},t+1) (10)

A low-risk MAS is one where if there exists a channel from sis_{i} to sjs_{j}, then ℐ⁡(si)⊆ℐ⁡(sj)\mathcal{I}(s_{i})\subseteq\mathcal{I}(s_{j}), so sjs_{j} would eventually learn anything that sis_{i} could tell them. However, sjs_{j} may still learn information earlier than they should; this affects pure coordination games, as agents could communicate their choice covertly, allowing guaranteed coordination. Formally, a low-risk MAS satisfies:

∀C⁡(si,sj),I⁡(si)⊆I⁡(sj)∧∃C⁡(si,sj),∃t≥0,∃x​s.t.​x∈I⁡(si,t)∧x∉I⁡(sj,t+1)\forall C(s_{i},s_{j}),\;I(s_{i})\subseteq I(s_{j})\quad\wedge\quad\exists C(s_{i},s_{j}),\,\exists t\geq 0,\,\exists x\;\text{s.t.}\;x\in I(s_{i},t)\,\wedge\,x\notin I(s_{j},t+1) (11)

A MAS has moderate-risk when illegal information flow could result in an agent learning information that they never should, but that information isn’t sensitive, or the receiving agent isn’t part of a critical system that may cause societal harm. Future introduction of sensitive information or changes to the system that increase its impact raises the potential for harm without developer consideration. Formally, a moderate-risk MAS satisfies:

∃C⁡(si,sj),ℐ⁡(si)⊈ℐ⁡(sj)\exists C(s_{i},s_{j}),\mathcal{I}(s_{i})\not\subseteq\mathcal{I}(s_{j}) (12)

A high-risk MAS is one where agents can receive information that they shouldn’t via illegal information flow, and either this information is sensitive, or the receiver is a component of a critical system. If steganography emerges in a high-risk system, the information set specification breaks down; in the worst case, the threat is equivalent to a single agent with the union of all inputs and outputs accessible by agents. Additionally, strict information sets typically only exist in systems where some combination of input/output channels may cause harm; thus, in high-risk environments, sharpness must be minimised. Formally, a high-risk MAS satisfies Equation 12 and:

∃x∈ℐ⁡(si)​ where ​x​ is considered sensitive∨sj​ is in a critical system\exists x\in\mathcal{I}(s_{i})\text{ where }x\text{ is considered sensitive}\lor s_{j}\text{ is in a critical system} (13)

4 Experiments

4.1 Agent implementations

For each environment variation, we use an instance of Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026) on Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025a) with the –dangerously-skip-permissions tag (Hughes, 2026) on a virtual machine. Both the task and paper are contained in the file system accessible to the agent, along with a virtual environment containing the necessary packages, and a file containing model log probabilities with some example usage code. The agent is prompted, “Follow the instructions in task.md”, the contents of which are shown in Figure 7, then left to implement autonomously until it terminates. The sub-model provided was small, and thus could be run on a CPU, not requiring any GPU compute.

In each experiment, the agent is provided with the paper by Zamir (2024) unless otherwise stated. Specific experiment variation and implementation details are shown in Appendix D. Implementation correctness was assessed by an instance of Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026) required to perform comprehensive tests and a complete evaluation; see Appendix C for prompt information. Initial implementations were also reviewed manually to ensure the correctness of the core result.

We found that in the default threat model described in Section 3.1, agents can successfully implement undetectable steganographic schemes, including with access to a paper describing an alternative scheme by Schroeder de Witt et al. (2023). The agent was also successful when the initial environment was empty: without immediate access to a sub-model to sample from, the agent introduced one itself, highlighting its ability to add complex artefacts to achieve a complete and correct scheme. We then changed the initial environment to be a generic MAS, where sub-model access was contained within the existing implementation, and gave the agent the additional task of attempting to hide its implementation in the MAS such that another developer couldn’t detect it. The agent succeeded, although it implemented a different scheme than the one in the paper we gave it, and an Opus 4.6 monitor couldn’t detect the presence of a fully functional stegosystem. In another experiment, we relaxed the requirement that an implementation description is contained in the agent’s file system; the agent used a web search to find the instructed paper and successfully implemented the scheme. The only experiment where we didn’t obtain a positive result was attempting to inject the malicious prompt in the research paper, providing the agent with an innocuous prompt instead. We expect that, given more extensive testing or specific prompt injection techniques tailored to the agent, this defence would prove fallible.

4.2 Coordination in multi-agent systems

We adapt the code from Aharon et al. (2026) by adding a steganography planning experiment, where the agent is instructed to implement a steganographic system to communicate with a partner; agents are told the problem specification and to return their chosen scheme, including their exact hyperparameters and design choices, along with their reasoning. Outputs are then fed into two instances of Opus 4.6, one categorising the chosen schemas and hyperparameters to identify successful cooperation in batches of 10, and one asserting that if another agent copied the scheme exactly, it would succeed, in batches of 5. Initial LLM outputs were checked manually to ensure correctness. The categories are then used to calculate ACI, HCI and CCI. The models use API-based inference, meaning no GPU compute is required, though the adapted code base does support local models. We vary the environment by changing the prompt in the following axes, experimenting using a 2×2×22\times 2\times 2 factorial.

  • •

    Undetectability - We either tell the agents that they must implement a computationally undetectable scheme, or that this is not necessary.

  • •

    Shared Secret Key/Public Key Infrastructure - We either tell agents that they share a secret key with the other agent, or that there is a public key infrastructure they can access.

  • •

    Common Knowledge - We either explicitly tell agents the common knowledge base, or that they have access to that information without mentioning the other agents’ information set.

Limited by tokens, we fixed N=100N=100 samples per agent, which ensured coordination instances occurred for most environments; thus, CCI is a reasonable approximation to Schelling sharpness. We advise practitioners that our results where CCI is 0 are not conclusive, and a larger sample size could lead to non-zero complete coordination. Each agent was run on every environment in our factorial; the performance in each metric by model is shown in Figure 1. The effects of each environment on each model for the success rate are shown in Figure 2, and for the CCI in Figure 3, where the error bars are the standard error of the mean for experiments with that condition.

The results broadly show that implementation success rate and each metric for the rate of coordination correspond to the model’s ability. Importantly, the models failed to register a non-zero CCI in any undetectable environment: coordination was typically avoided by the presence of some parameter that they never coordinated on; hence, the CCI contribution for those algorithms was 0. Notably, Haiku maintains impressively high algorithmic and hyperparameter coordination, considering the model size; this is likely due to less variety of algorithmic knowledge, resulting in a high rate of coordination. The trend of success rate mimics the model sizes; the success rate of Opus in the coordination runs is surprisingly high, given that it has no tool access.

4.3 Mitigations

Agents with access to tools proved very effective at implementing stegosystems, highlighting the dangers of unmonitored tool use. The most effective mitigation is to monitor tool usage and to move away from methods that skip permissions. Another effective but computationally expensive method is to crowd the common knowledge base with similar implementation descriptions, reducing the Schelling sharpness by introducing new, similarly salient Nash equilibria; an exponential number of descriptions need to be included to ensure a negligible chance of coordination. For the MAS experiments, we found that agents with no tool usage coordinate effectively on most hyperparameters, but cannot coordinate completely on undetectable schemes; hence, using monitors between agents reduces the threat posed by steganography.

4.4 Limitations

Sample size.

A key limitation of our implementation experiments is the very small sample size. Each experiment had long setup, implementation, and verification times, and as such a large sample size was infeasible. This is also a limitation of the coordination experiments, caused by a restriction on available tokens: we provide a lower bound for CCI, but with a larger sample size, many instances where some hyperparameter probability was 0 in our experiment would contribute to the CCI. We also didn’t provide agents with tool access for these experiments, as it was beyond the scope of our research, but repeating experiments with web and PDF tools would likely raise the CCI significantly.

Model scope.

We also only used Anthropic models in these experiments; thus, our claims only apply directly to those, though we would expect them to generalise to LLMs from other providers.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we evaluated the limiting factor of agentic covert communication by separating the problem into steganographic implementations and tacit coordination on stegosystems. Empirically, we demonstrated that under reasonable tool affordances, frontier agentic models can operationalise varied stegosystems, including ones that are computationally undetectable or perfectly secure. We also demonstrated that complete successful coordination without prior communication or tool usage is non-negligible under reasonable circumstances. Both our formulation for Schelling sharpness and coordination metrics apply to future coordination games research. Similarly, our discussion on information flow and risk can be flexibly applied to other research on monitored-channel systems.

Long-term alignment and high-stakes research.

The highest-stakes setting for this threat may not be ordinary chatbot interaction, but automated safety-critical research itself. Future frontier-AI safety cases may depend on AI agents reading papers, writing evaluation code, auditing logs, red-teaming deployments, maintaining shared workspaces, and producing evidence that determines whether more capable systems are safe to train or deploy (Buhl et al., 2024; Greenblatt et al., 2024; Korbak et al., 2025). In such settings, our results suggest that once agents can use tools, the relevant question is no longer only whether a monitor can read their final messages, but whether the whole research environment prevents illicit information flow through messages, code, and shared artefacts. Even low-bandwidth covert channels could let agents coordinate research directions, bypass staged access controls, or collude in audits. Long term, we hope this work helps move agentic AI safety from ad hoc message monitoring toward information-flow assurance for high-stakes multi-agent systems: safety cases should argue not only that each agent is individually monitored, but that the surrounding tool-mediated organisation remains robust to covert coordination.

Appendix A Steganography introduction

Steganography is the technique of hiding information such that its presence is undetectable [Cachin, 1998], for example, by hiding a message within an innocuous cover. When two parties share some secret information, they can create a secret key stegosystem:

Definition 7

A secret key stegosystem [Katzenbeisser and Petitcolas, 2000] is the quintuple

𝕊=⟨C,M,K,DK,EK⟩\mathbb{S}=\langle C,M,K,D_{K},E_{K}\rangle where CC is the set of possible covers, MM is the set of secret messages with |M|≤|C||M|\leq|C|, KK is the set of secret keys, EK:C×M×K→CE_{K}:C\times M\times K\to C is the embedding function, and DK:C×K→MD_{K}:C\times K\to M is the decoding function, satisfying the property that ∀m∈M,∀c∈C,∀k∈K,D⁡(E⁡(c,m,k),k)=m\forall m\in M,\forall c\in C,\forall k\in K,\;D(E(c,m,k),k)=m.

This is demonstrated effectively by the “Prisoners’ Problem" by Simmons [1984] in Figure 4.

Typically, the cover space contains only inconspicuous covers, and the stego-object generated by the embedding function must be perceptually similar to the cover, so Eve doesn’t suspect anything untoward [Katzenbeisser and Petitcolas, 2000].

A simple stegosystem is an acrostic, where the hidden message is encoded as the first letter of consecutive words or sentences, as shown in Figure 5.

A.1 Undetectability

Steganography hides the existence of messages, but different schemes have different levels of detectability to different observers. For example, the payload within the acrostic shown in Figure 5 is undetectable to most people reading the passage, but not to someone told to look for acrostic messages.

Definition 8

Let CC be a non-empty cover set and aa be some actor who attempts to distinguish between covers. Their similarity function is s​i​ma:C×C→(0,1]sim_{a}:C\times C\to(0,1], where s​i​ma​(x,y)=1sim_{a}(x,y)=1 iff actor aa perceives no difference between covers x,yx,y.

Thus, if Alice and Bob know that Eve has the similarity function s​i​mesim_{e}, choosing a stegosystem that is perceptually undetectable to Eve ensures that Eve never detects their covert communications.

Definition 9

A stegosystem 𝕊=⟨C,M,K,DK,EK⟩\mathbb{S}=\langle C,M,K,D_{K},E_{K}\rangle is ϵ\epsilon-perceptually-undetectable to actor aa for some ϵ∈[0,1)\epsilon\in[0,1) iff:

∀m∈M,∀c∈C,∀k∈K,s​i​ma​(c,E⁡(c,m,k))≥1−ϵ\forall m\in M,\forall c\in C,\forall k\in K,\;\;sim_{a}(c,E(c,m,k))\geq 1-\epsilon

When ϵ=0\epsilon=0, we say 𝕊\mathbb{S} is perceptually undetectable to aa.

However, in most scenarios, either Alice and Bob don’t know s​i​mesim_{e}, or there is no perceptually undetectable stegosystem for an actor. We instead consider stegosystems that are computationally undetectable:

Definition 10

Fix a cover generator GG to be some function that generates covers c∈Cc\in C. Let the key kk be some value in K={0,1}λK=\{0,1\}^{\lambda} where λ\lambda is a security parameter representing the key length. Define a polynomial-time adversary AA, where A⁡(G,x)A(G,x) represents that AA can query cover generator GG and compare the outputs with xx, and A⁡(G,x)=1A(G,x)=1 means they have determined whether xx can be drawn from GG. A stegosystem is computationally undetectable [Zamir, 2024] if for all messages mm, and all adversaries AA:

|ℙ[A(G,c)=1]−ℙk←{0,1}λ[A(G,E(c,m,k))=1]|≤1λn∀n>1\left\lvert\mathbb{P}[A(G,c)=1]-\mathbb{P}_{k\leftarrow\{0,1\}^{\lambda}}[A(G,E(c,m,k))=1]\right\rvert\leq\frac{1}{\lambda^{n}}\quad\forall n>1

In the case of LLM steganography, the cover generator GG is the model itself.

The best that Alice and Bob can achieve is a perfectly secure stegosystem that is information-theoretically undetectable to any monitor [Schroeder de Witt et al., 2023]:

Definition 11

Fix a secret key stegosystem 𝕊=⟨C,M,K,DK,EK⟩\mathbb{S}=\langle C,M,K,D_{K},E_{K}\rangle. Define the set of stego-objects S={s∣∃c∈C,∃m∈M,∃k∈KS=\{s\mid\exists c\in C,\exists m\in M,\exists k\in K s.t E(c,m,k)=s}E(c,m,k)=s\}. Then 𝕊\mathbb{S} is perfectly secure if K​L​(C,S)=0KL(C,S)=0, i.e. the KL divergence between the cover and stego-object distributions is zero Cachin [1998].

A.2 Steganography in LLMs

LLM outputs can be adjusted to encode a payload. A simple method that is perceptually undetectable to humans is zero-width encoding; different Unicode characters with no width can be used to hide a payload without visually changing the cover [Bashir et al., 2020], as shown in Figure 6.

LLMs can choose a mapping of zero-width Unicode characters to sequences of bits which represent portions of ASCII characters, thus hiding an ASCII message in their ordinary outputs that is invisible to humans but decodable by other LLMs. This is therefore not secure in the presence of a monitor where zero-width encoding is perceptually detectable (i.e. another LLM that can see the zero-width characters).

A more complex computationally undetectable stegosystem plants a payload in the LLM response by adapting a watermarking algorithm that doesn’t alter the distribution of responses [Christ et al., 2023]. A shared secret key is required to extract the payload from the model’s response; crucially, without the key, it is provably impossible to distinguish between the original LLM responses and the responses containing the payload [Zamir, 2024]. Algorithm 1 shows the core method; we refer readers to Zamir [2024] for more details regarding the adaptation for the watermarking algorithm, including information about pseudorandom functions (PRF) and dynamic error-correcting codes (ECCs) used in Algorithm 1, and to Christ et al. [2023] for a proof of undetectability.

A.3 Consequences

A steganographic channel can be used for illegal information flow in a MAS, even with the presence of a monitor, subverting the model specification and allowing some subject sjs_{j} to obtain information x∉ℐ⁡(sj)x\not\in\mathcal{I}(s_{j}). If xx is sensitive information, and sjs_{j} is in a critical system that shouldn’t have access to xx, the system may cause serious harm. For example, if sjs_{j} can output to users and shouldn’t be permitted to access personally identifiable information xx, i.e. x∉ℐ⁡(sj)x\not\in\mathcal{I}(s_{j}), but a subject sis_{i} with x∈ℐ⁡(si)x\in\mathcal{I}(s_{i}) establishes a steganographic channel C⁡(si,sj)C(s_{i},s_{j}), a monitor sms_{m} is incapable of identifying the illegal information flow of xx being sent to sjs_{j}, thus the information can be incorrectly output, potentially causing societal harm. Another example is that models may collude via the covert channel to perpetuate biases [Motwani et al., 2025].

Steganography can be damaging even when an agent doesn’t exist within a MAS, or when it is in an isolated environment without internet access. For example. using the undetectable scheme, an LLM (even one running offline) with access to sensitive information could hide it in its responses, so anyone with the secret key who sees the innocuous outputs could obtain it later [Zamir, 2024].

Appendix B Extended related work

B.1 Misalignment

AI alignment is concerned with ensuring AI systems behave in line with human intentions and values [Ji et al., 2025]; preventing malicious behaviour becomes more essential as AI capabilities, and thus, risks from misalignment, grow. Since, by definition, emergent steganography is unintended by the system designer, if agents were perfectly aligned with the developer’s intentions, such behaviour wouldn’t occur; reducing misalignment is a key approach to reducing steganography. Standard training objectives for LLMs of next word prediction [Radford et al., 2019] or determining contextual similarity of sentences [Devlin et al., 2019] aren’t necessarily in line with human values [Shen et al., 2023]; additional interventions are required for alignment. However, specifying human values is intrinsically difficult due to cultural variations; a popular view is that LLMs should be helpful, honest and harmless (known colloquially as triple H) [Askell et al., 2021]. Most successful methods employ reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) [Christiano et al., 2017], for example, using human preferences as a reward signal in fine-tuning by having labellers rank outputs [Ouyang et al., 2022]. Despite this, frontier LLMs can exhibit extreme misalignment, highlighted by a recent example, where an LLM resorted to blackmail, espionage, and lethal action when presented with a conflict of goals or threatened with replacement [Lynch et al., 2025]. Additionally, fine-tuning models on a narrow malicious objective can induce broad misalignment, unrelated to the objective [Betley et al., 2025], showing that current alignment methods are fragile and vulnerable to backdoors. Misalignment can be measured with safety benchmarks by simulating tool usage in common environments, tracking different categories of risks to ensure broad alignment is recorded [Zhang et al., 2025a, Zhang et al., 2025b, Chen et al., 2024].

Despite the improved utility of using a MAS, it can exhibit greater misalignment with the system goal than single agents [Shen et al., 2026], and team misalignment may arise from agents with varied goals or intentions that conflict with each other or with the system’s goal. Conflict between agents resembles contending opinions in human populations [Kierans et al., 2022], which can be quantified as the probability of misalignment given a population and problem area [Jang et al., 2017], meaning team misalignment in large, diverse agent groups with potentially conflicting goals across various problems can be calculated [Kierans et al., 2025]. Social conventions, including collective bias and system misalignment not present in individual models, can be amplified, induced, or overridden by playing simple coordination games, coordinating differently than a single model on a cultural bias when presented with two options [Flint et al., 2025, Ashery et al., 2025]. For mixed-motive games, team alignment can be improved through an optimisation method that progressively aligns individual and collective objectives [Li et al., 2024]. For general problems, methods of reducing team misalignment often resort to social scenarios that would typically reduce misalignment in human populations [Ashery et al., 2025], introducing frameworks like debate [Irving et al., 2018, Estornell and Liu, 2024]; these improve factuality and reasoning [Du et al., 2023] by promoting divergent thinking [Liang et al., 2023].

In this project, we explore how unintended steganographic collusion between LLMs can emerge due to misspecified training reward incentives [Mathew et al., 2025]. This is a form of reward hacking: a type of misalignment where agents undergoing an optimisation process, such as training, exploit gaps in a misspecified reward function, thereby finding an unintended solution and obtaining the reward without necessarily achieving the objective [Pan et al., 2022]. Training on documents that inform agents about reward hacking induces the behaviour [Hu et al., 2025]; but even without this, frontier LLMs frequently engage in sophisticated reward hacking behaviour, for example, in autonomous software development, they attempt to modify tests, exploit loopholes and bugs, and gain access to existing implementations [Von Arx et al., 2025]. Mitigation typically requires a monitor observing the chain of thought (CoT) reasoning to determine agent intent; however, with extreme optimisation or strict restrictions on undesired reasoning, agents can learn to obfuscate their intent from the monitor within their CoT while reward hacking at a significant rate [Baker et al., 2025, Skaf et al., 2025].

B.2 Watermarking

Originally a method to protect the copyright of digital media, watermarking robustly hides information about the object it is within [Katzenbeisser and Petitcolas, 2000]. Both watermarking and steganography imperceptibly convey information by embedding it in covers, but are distinct fields, as watermarking requires a high level of robustness against attacks to prevent the removal of the watermark [Katzenbeisser and Petitcolas, 2000]. Due to their inherent similarities, steganographic algorithms utilise many mathematical primitives common in watermarking algorithms, such as pseudorandom functions (PRFs) [Goldreich et al., 1986] used to spread the hidden information throughout the cover in a way that appears random, and error correcting codes (ECCs) used for robustness in watermarking [Christ and Gunn, 2024] and for increasing the efficiency of embeddings in steganography [Munuera, 2007]. Consequently, numerous steganographic methods are developed concurrently with watermarking methods [Evsutin et al., 2020, Wang et al., 2023].

Given the potential for LLMs to generate illegal and explicit content, with AI-generated child abuse imagery more than doubling between 2024 and 2025 [Kendall MP and Phillips MP, 2025], the ease of generating and spreading falsehoods or emotional distress [Grinbaum and Adomaitis, 2022], and the increasingly imperceptible distinction between AI-generated content and real life, even to advanced algorithmic detectors with access to image metadata [Ghiurău and Popescu, 2025, Elkhatat et al., 2023], a watermark for LLM-generated content is extremely valuable. In particular, we desire a fingerprint where the embedded watermark specifies metadata that determines the author of the data [Katzenbeisser and Petitcolas, 2000]. Fortunately, there is extensive research into embedding watermarks in AI-generated content for different purposes. There exist watermarks for text-based outputs, detectable using efficient open-source algorithms [Kirchenbauer et al., 2024, Fernandez et al., 2023] and undetectable without a secret key [Christ et al., 2023, Boroujeny et al., 2024]; and for image outputs, remaining undetectable without a secret key [Gunn et al., 2024]. Major LLM providers originally pledged to watermark content for safety [Bartz et al., 2023], but real-world deployment remains limited, likely due to misaligned incentives between LLM providers and end users [Liu et al., 2026].

B.3 LLM cooperation

LLMs exhibit strong coordination capabilities in general scenarios [Zhu et al., 2025], but without an imposed organisational structure, their helpful nature leads to over-reporting and unnecessary compliance [Guo et al., 2024]; the benefits of structure are exhibited in real-life applications like a MAS-operated vending machine [Anthropic, 2025b]. A tacit coordination game is a pure coordination game with multiple Nash equilibria; rational decision makers cannot be certain about which equilibrium action other players will use [Huyck et al., 1990]. LLMs have remarkable abilities in tacit coordination games, but often struggle in common-sense coordination involving numbers or cultural archetypes [Aharon et al., 2026]. Additionally, LLMs perform well in extended self-interested games [Akata et al., 2025] such as the iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma family [Robinson and Goforth, 2006].

Advanced cooperative reasoning problems require Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning - the ability to understand that other people have their own thoughts [Ruhl, 2025], thus LLMs must predict the intentions of their partners [Agashe et al., 2025]. Despite early research suggesting that LLMs possess ToM [Kosinski, 2023, Strickland, 2024, Strachan et al., 2024], recent results highlight deficiencies in LLM social reasoning abilities [Amirizaniani et al., 2024, Agashe et al., 2025], implying that ToM is likely mimicked by reflection of pre-training data [Aharon et al., 2026, Kosinski, 2023]. ToM reasoning can be improved by integrating human intentions and using emotive language [Amirizaniani et al., 2024], by explicitly representing agent beliefs [Li et al., 2023], or by inferring and propagating weighted hypotheses about agents’ thoughts [Kim et al., 2025].

Appendix C Prompts

Figure 7 contains the prompt used to initiate steganographic implementation in the implementation experiment. We verified the implementations using the prompt contained in Figure 8.

Figure 9 and Figure 10 contain prompts used to specify experiments within the factorial for the multi-agent testing. We don’t provide all prompts for the 8 experiments, as the others are formed from different aspects of those two.

Appendix D Agent-implemented steganographic scheme details

Table 1 shows the detailed implementation descriptions from the experiments of agent implementations. The results broadly indicate a strong ability to implement steganographic schemes. Most implementations contained minor bugs that caused failures on edge cases, but were successful otherwise. The failed runs on experiment 1.1 were due to the agent changing the scheme to require the prompt to decode the message. The failed runs on experiment 2 were because agents actively resisted the prompt injection. In experiment 4, an Opus 4.6 monitor couldn’t identify that some steganographic scheme had been implemented when viewing the code base.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The abstract and introduction state that agentic coding models can produce undetectable stegosystems with a variety of realistic tool usage, including when required to adapt to missing ingredients; this is justified by our experiments in Section 4.1. We also claim that by framing steganographic coordination as a Schelling point problem, we demonstrate that covert communication is a present-day threat; this is justified by our results from the experiments in Section 4.2, showing high levels of coordination on most aspects of implementations, and non-negligible levels of perfect successful coordination.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: We include the key limitation of the small sample size in Section 4.4 dedicated to limitations.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [N/A]

  14. Justification: The paper is empirical and doesn’t present any theoretical results. We introduce coordination metrics, but don’t make any theoretical claims about them, and explain their creation in Section 3.2.1.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: The paper describes the models used and detailed experiment setups, including the prompts used in Section C.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

  21. 5.

    Open access to data and code

  22. Question: Does the paper provide open access to the data and code, with sufficient instructions to faithfully reproduce the main experimental results, as described in supplemental material?

  23. Answer: [Yes]

  24. Justification: For the implementation experiments, we provide the prompts used in C, specify our setup in 4.1, and provide access to the default setup in the supplementary materials. For the coordination experiments, our code, adapted from Aharon et al. [2026], is contained in the supplementary materials.

  25. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that paper does not include experiments requiring code.

    • •

      Please see the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      While we encourage the release of code and data, we understand that this might not be possible, so [No] is an acceptable answer. Papers cannot be rejected simply for not including code, unless this is central to the contribution (e.g., for a new open-source benchmark).

    • •

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

    • •

      The authors should provide instructions on data access and preparation, including how to access the raw data, preprocessed data, intermediate data, and generated data, etc.

    • •

      The authors should provide scripts to reproduce all experimental results for the new proposed method and baselines. If only a subset of experiments are reproducible, they should state which ones are omitted from the script and why.

    • •

      At submission time, to preserve anonymity, the authors should release anonymized versions (if applicable).

    • •

      Providing as much information as possible in supplemental material (appended to the paper) is recommended, but including URLs to data and code is permitted.

  26. 6.

    Experimental setting/details

  27. Question: Does the paper specify all the training and test details (e.g., data splits, hyperparameters, how they were chosen, type of optimizer) necessary to understand the results?

  28. Answer: [Yes]

  29. Justification: The core details are the prompts used to initiate implementations and implementation plans, which are contained in Appendix C.

  30. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The experimental setting should be presented in the core of the paper to a level of detail that is necessary to appreciate the results and make sense of them.

    • •

      The full details can be provided either with the code, in appendix, or as supplemental material.

  31. 7.

    Experiment statistical significance

  32. Question: Does the paper report error bars suitably and correctly defined or other appropriate information about the statistical significance of the experiments?

  33. Answer: [Yes]

  34. Justification: The only error bars present are contained in Figure 2 and 3; we explain that they represent the standard error of the mean for experiments with that condition in Section 4.2. Error bars aren’t required in Figure 1 as each point on the graph represents one of our calculated coordination metrics.

  35. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The authors should answer [Yes] if the results are accompanied by error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests, at least for the experiments that support the main claims of the paper.

    • •

      The factors of variability that the error bars are capturing should be clearly stated (for example, train/test split, initialization, random drawing of some parameter, or overall run with given experimental conditions).

    • •

      The method for calculating the error bars should be explained (closed form formula, call to a library function, bootstrap, etc.)

    • •

      The assumptions made should be given (e.g., Normally distributed errors).

    • •

      It should be clear whether the error bar is the standard deviation or the standard error of the mean.

    • •

      It is OK to report 1-sigma error bars, but one should state it. The authors should preferably report a 2-sigma error bar than state that they have a 96% CI, if the hypothesis of Normality of errors is not verified.

    • •

      For asymmetric distributions, the authors should be careful not to show in tables or figures symmetric error bars that would yield results that are out of range (e.g., negative error rates).

    • •

      If error bars are reported in tables or plots, the authors should explain in the text how they were calculated and reference the corresponding figures or tables in the text.

  36. 8.

    Experiments compute resources

  37. Question: For each experiment, does the paper provide sufficient information on the computer resources (type of compute workers, memory, time of execution) needed to reproduce the experiments?

  38. Answer: [Yes]

  39. Justification: We use API-based inference and describe this in Section 4.1 and Section 4.2. No model training or fine-tuning was performed.

  40. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      The paper should indicate the type of compute workers CPU or GPU, internal cluster, or cloud provider, including relevant memory and storage.

    • •

      The paper should provide the amount of compute required for each of the individual experimental runs as well as estimate the total compute.

    • •

      The paper should disclose whether the full research project required more compute than the experiments reported in the paper (e.g., preliminary or failed experiments that didn’t make it into the paper).

  41. 9.

    Code of ethics

  42. Question: Does the research conducted in the paper conform, in every respect, with the NeurIPS Code of Ethics https://neurips.cc/public/EthicsGuidelines?

  43. Answer: [Yes]

  44. Justification: Our work is intended to raise awareness of the safety concern so that future practitioners can implement effective mitigations. Section 4.3 highlights some of these approaches, focusing on the necessity of a monitor, and providing other suggestions for when undetectable schemes are possible.

  45. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the authors have not reviewed the NeurIPS Code of Ethics.

    • •

      If the authors answer [No] , they should explain the special circumstances that require a deviation from the Code of Ethics.

    • •

      The authors should make sure to preserve anonymity (e.g., if there is a special consideration due to laws or regulations in their jurisdiction).

  46. 10.

    Broader impacts

  47. Question: Does the paper discuss both potential positive societal impacts and negative societal impacts of the work performed?

  48. Answer: [Yes]

  49. Justification: The paper discusses the societal goals and impacts of this research in Section 5, focusing on the dangers of steganography that we highlight.

  50. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that there is no societal impact of the work performed.

    • •

      If the authors answer [N/A] or [No] , they should explain why their work has no societal impact or why the paper does not address societal impact.

    • •

      Examples of negative societal impacts include potential malicious or unintended uses (e.g., disinformation, generating fake profiles, surveillance), fairness considerations (e.g., deployment of technologies that could make decisions that unfairly impact specific groups), privacy considerations, and security considerations.

    • •

      The conference expects that many papers will be foundational research and not tied to particular applications, let alone deployments. However, if there is a direct path to any negative applications, the authors should point it out. For example, it is legitimate to point out that an improvement in the quality of generative models could be used to generate Deepfakes for disinformation. On the other hand, it is not needed to point out that a generic algorithm for optimizing neural networks could enable people to train models that generate Deepfakes faster.

    • •

      The authors should consider possible harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended and functioning correctly, harms that could arise when the technology is being used as intended but gives incorrect results, and harms following from (intentional or unintentional) misuse of the technology.

    • •

      If there are negative societal impacts, the authors could also discuss possible mitigation strategies (e.g., gated release of models, providing defenses in addition to attacks, mechanisms for monitoring misuse, mechanisms to monitor how a system learns from feedback over time, improving the efficiency and accessibility of ML).

  51. 11.

    Safeguards

  52. Question: Does the paper describe safeguards that have been put in place for responsible release of data or models that have a high risk for misuse (e.g., pre-trained language models, image generators, or scraped datasets)?

  53. Answer: [N/A]

  54. Justification: The paper doesn’t introduce any new datasets or models.

  55. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper poses no such risks.

    • •

      Released models that have a high risk for misuse or dual-use should be released with necessary safeguards to allow for controlled use of the model, for example by requiring that users adhere to usage guidelines or restrictions to access the model or implementing safety filters.

    • •

      Datasets that have been scraped from the Internet could pose safety risks. The authors should describe how they avoided releasing unsafe images.

    • •

      We recognize that providing effective safeguards is challenging, and many papers do not require this, but we encourage authors to take this into account and make a best faith effort.

    • •

      If this information is not available online, the authors are encouraged to reach out to the asset’s creators.
